Make a map. Change one setting. Watch the story change.

A one-hour QGIS session in three maps. The same data can tell different stories — the number you get depends on the choices you make.

  • Task 1 · Aichi Hands-on, 25 min. Build a map of foreign permanent residents in every municipality.
  • Task 2 · One hospital Tour, 15 min. Who lives within a 10-minute walk of Kawashima Hospital?
  • Task 3 · Moriyama Ward Slides, 7 min. How many residents can walk to a hospital in 10, 20 or 30 minutes?

Start here

The hour

  • Introduction: 5 min
  • Task 1, hands-on: 25 min
  • Task 2, tour: 15 min
  • Task 3, slides: 7 min
  • Limits: 6 min
  • Wrap-up: 2 min

What you need

  • QGIS 3.44 is recommended; other versions work, but menus differ slightly.
  • Two data files for Task 1: boundaries and residents table.
  • An internet connection for the base map.
  • Task 2 and 3 files are in the repository folder.

Where the data come from

  • Boundaries (N03) and hospitals (P04): MLIT National Land Numerical Information, P04.
  • Population grid: 2020 Census, e-Stat.
  • Foreign residents: Statistics on Foreign Residents, e-Stat, December 2025.
  • Roads and walking: OpenStreetMap contributors.
  • Base map: GSI tiles. Municipality codes: Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications.

Task 1 · Foreign permanent residents in Aichi

Goal: build a colour-coded map of Aichi from a plain table of numbers, then change one setting and watch the story change. About 25 minutes, done together.

Menu names follow QGIS 3.44; other versions differ slightly.

What you need

  • aichi_admin_fields2025.geojson — municipality boundaries of Aichi (MLIT N03, 1 January 2025).
  • aichi_permanent_residents_202512.csv — one row per municipality (Nagoya: per ward): city_code, pr_all, pr_brazil, pr_korea.

pr_all counts foreigners with the status permanent resident (永住者). pr_brazil is the part of them with Brazilian nationality. Both files share a 5-digit municipality code: 23201 is 23 (Aichi) + 201 (Toyohashi). That code is the key that lets you join them.

1 · Base map

  1. Choose Layer ▸ Add Layer ▸ Add XYZ Layer…. The Data Source Manager opens on the XYZ tab.
  2. Click New.
  3. Name: GSI standard
  4. URL: https://cyberjapandata.gsi.go.jp/xyz/std/{z}/{x}/{y}.png
  5. Min. Zoom level: 5. Click OK.
  6. Select GSI standard in the list, click Add, then Close.

2 · Municipality polygons

  1. Drag aichi_admin_fields2025.geojson into the QGIS window.
  2. Right-click the new layer ▸ Open Attribute Table.
  3. Find the column N03_007: it is the municipality code. There are more rows than municipalities, because islands and exclaves are separate polygons. One row, 23000, is the unassigned area (所属未定地).

3 · Join the numbers

  1. Drag aichi_permanent_residents_202512.csv into the QGIS window. It appears as a table without a map.
  2. Double-click the polygon layer to open its Properties, then choose Joins.
  3. Click the green +.
  4. Join layer: the CSV. Join field: city_code. Target field: N03_007.
  5. Leave the other settings as they are and click OK.
  6. Open the attribute table again. The CSV columns are attached with the layer name as a prefix: aichi_permanent_residents_202512_pr_all, aichi_permanent_residents_202512_pr_brazil, and so on.

If every joined value is empty, the two key fields differ in type (number vs. text). Check both in the attribute table.

4 · Turn text into numbers

The joined numbers are left-aligned in the attribute table: QGIS read the CSV columns as text. Text cannot be coloured by size, so make number fields from them.

  1. Select the polygon layer and open its Field Calculator (Ctrl+I; ⌘+I on a Mac).
  2. Tick Create virtual field. Output field name: pr_all. Type: Whole number (integer).
  3. Expression: to_int("aichi_permanent_residents_202512_pr_all"). Pick the field from Fields and Values in the middle list rather than typing it. Click OK.
  4. Repeat for pr_brazil with to_int("aichi_permanent_residents_202512_pr_brazil").

The new fields are right-aligned: they are numbers now. The unassigned area 23000 stays empty (NULL), not 0.

5 · Colour by number

  1. Open the layer Properties ▸ Symbology. At the top, change Single Symbol to Graduated.
  2. Value: pr_brazil. Pick a colour ramp. Classes: 5.
  3. Click Classify, then OK.

Surprise 1 — the classes decide the picture. With the default Equal Interval, almost every municipality lands in the lowest colour. Reopen Symbology and change Mode to Equal Count (Quantile), click Classify. Then try Natural Breaks (Jenks). Same data, three different maps. No mode is neutral, so say which one you used.

  • Equal Interval cuts the range from lowest to highest value into classes of equal width. A few very large values stretch the range, so most places end up in the first class.
  • Equal Count (Quantile) puts the same number of municipalities into each class. Every colour shows up, but two places with almost the same value can get different colours.
  • Natural Breaks (Jenks) sets the class limits at the biggest gaps in the data, so values within a class are as close to each other as possible. The limits change with the data, so two Jenks maps cannot be compared directly.

6 · From counts to rates

  1. Open the Field Calculator again.
  2. Tick Create virtual field. Output field name: rate_brazil. Type: Decimal number (real).
  3. Expression: "pr_brazil" / "pr_all" * 100. Click OK.
  4. Back in Symbology, set Value to rate_brazil and click Classify.

Surprise 2 — counts mostly show where many people live. By count the top three are Toyohashi (豊橋市, 4,182), Toyota (豊田市, 3,563) and Nishio (西尾市, 2,491). By share of all permanent residents the lead goes to Hekinan (碧南市, 64%), Shinshiro (新城市, 62%) and Toyone (豊根村, 60%). Toyone is 6 of 10 people.

7 · Export (optional)

  1. Project ▸ New Print Layout. Add a Map, a Legend, a Scale bar and a Title.
  2. Layout ▸ Export as Image.

Before you export: legend labels should read like words, not pr_brazil. Keep the base map pale so the data colours stand out. Put the source and date in the caption.

Watch out

  • Small numbers make wild rates. Shitara (設楽町) has 7 permanent residents in all; 3 Brazilians already read as 42.86%. Always look at the counts behind a rate.
  • Missing is not zero. The unassigned area 23000 has no data. It stays empty after the join and must not be coloured as 0.
  • Know what the category means. Permanent resident is one residence status. Special permanent residents (特別永住者) are a separate group and are not included.

More on what these maps can and cannot say: Limits.

    Task 2 · A 10-minute walk from one hospital

    Goal: answer one question — how many people live within a 10-minute walk of one hospital? The hospital is Kawashima Hospital (川島病院) in Moriyama Ward, Nagoya. About 15 minutes. Here the presenter opens a finished project and walks you through it: switch layers on and off, click objects, read the numbers.

    The layers

    All six files are in the repository. To follow along, drag them into a new QGIS project.

    • moriyama_admin_field.gpkg — the ward boundary.
    • moriyama_hospital_test.gpkg — one point: 川島病院.
    • moriyama_service_area_lines.gpkg — the roads you can walk along within 10 minutes (walking speed 4 km/h).
    • moriyama_test_10min_polygon_clean.gpkg — the 10-minute reach as an area.
    • moriyama_mesh_3km.gpkg — the 250 m population grid (2020 Census) around the ward: 2,745 cells.
    • moriyama_test_10min_intersection_with_population_clean.gpkg — only the grid cells inside the reach, cut to its edge: 20 pieces, each with an estimated population pop_est.

    The tour

    1. Switch on the ward boundary and the hospital point. Zoom to the hospital.
    2. Switch on the walkable roads. These are all the streets reachable on foot within 10 minutes. This is the line version of the answer.
    3. Switch on the 10-minute reach. It is a smoothed surface of walking time over the road network, cut at 10 minutes. It turns the lines into an area.
    4. Switch on the population grid, then the 20 pieces inside the reach. Choose the Identify Features tool and click a piece: pop_est is the estimated number of people living in that piece.
    5. Add up the 20 pieces:
      • Open the Processing Toolbox: Processing ▸ Toolbox (Ctrl/⌘+Alt+T). It opens as a panel on the right.
      • Type Basic statistics into the search field at the top of the panel. Double-click Basic statistics for fields (under Vector analysis).
      • Input layer: the layer with the 20 pieces. Field to calculate statistics on: pop_est. Click Run.
      • Read SUM in the result (the Log tab of the dialog, or the Results Viewer).
      The sum is 5,420.9 — about 5,421 people live within a 10-minute walk of 川島病院.

    How the number is made

    A grid cell that is only half inside the reach gets half of its population. This is called area apportioning. It assumes the people in a cell are spread evenly across it.

    The first run of this analysis gave about 6,878. Grid cells outside the reach had slipped into the sum. After the fix the answer fell by about 21%. It came to light only when the reach outline looked doubled on the map.

    Not the same as Task 3. This reach was built with a different method from the one in Task 3. Do not compare the two numbers.

    Watch out

    • Even spread inside each cell is an assumption. A cell with one apartment block and a park is not even.
    • The reach depends on the walking speed (4 km/h) and on which roads count as walkable.

      Task 3 · Walking access across Moriyama Ward

      Question: of all the people living in Moriyama Ward, what share can walk to at least one hospital in 10, 20 or 30 minutes? About 7 minutes, slides only — you will not repeat these steps today.

      10 min2030
      of Moriyama residents live within a -minute walk of a hospital

      Approximate, potential access — not actual use of care.

      Computed with a different method from Task 2 (a 30 m buffer around walkable roads, not a smoothed walking-time surface), so do not compare the two numbers.

      The result

      Walking timeResidents within reachShare
      10 min31,287.8017.90%
      20 min81,492.4146.61%
      30 min109,452.9362.60%

      All shares are out of 174,833.87 estimated residents of the ward. Numbers are estimates, so the decimals are not meant to be exact.

      Four steps

      1. Reach of each hospital. For each of 41 hospitals in or within 3 km of the ward, find the roads reachable on foot (4 km/h) within 10, 20 and 30 minutes. Draw a 30 m buffer around those roads.
      2. Dissolve. For each time, merge the 41 buffers into one shape. A person who lives near two hospitals is counted once.
      3. Clip. Cut the merged shape to the ward boundary.
      4. Count people. Use area apportioning on the 250 m population grid: people inside the shape divided by all people in the ward.

      Why Dissolve matters. Adding up the people near each hospital would count some residents several times. Merging first removes the overlaps.

      Approximate, potential access. These are estimates of who could walk to a hospital, based on roads and a buffer. They do not show who actually goes there, or whether a hospital can treat them. 62.60% is a result of this method, not a verified fact.

      This reach was built with a different method from Task 2 (a buffer around reachable roads instead of a smoothed walking-time surface), so do not compare the two numbers.

      Limits · What these numbers can and cannot say

      Every map today gave a number. Here is how far each number can be trusted — three limits, in plain words.

      1 · The 30 m buffer is an approximation

      The reach in Task 3 is not a true "30 minutes on foot" area. It takes the roads reachable on foot and draws a 30 m strip around them. A wider or narrower strip would give a different population. The walkable roads come from OpenStreetMap, selected by provisional rules, and nobody has checked that every crossing and connection works in real life. A small hole inside a reach is often just a block of houses away from the road, not a processing error.

      2 · Population is spread by area

      The population grid has 250 m cells, and a cell cut by a boundary is split by area, as if people were spread evenly. In reality they live in buildings. There is a second gap: 96 cells in the ward have no population value at all (NULL). By eye they sit on parks, rivers and woods, but the real reason, such as no residents, a suppressed value or a failed join, has not been checked. We did not turn them into 0. They are left out of the sums, so the shares are based on the cells that do have a value.

      3 · This is potential access, not use of care

      The question answered is "could a person walk to a hospital in this time?" It says nothing about who actually goes, whether the hospital has the right doctors, whether there is room for more patients, or how healthy people are. The list holds the 41 hospitals in or within 3 km of the ward, with no distinction by type or speciality. Read 62.60% as a potential, geographic share: a useful first look, not a finding.

      So what for your own research?

      Before you trust or publish a map, ask three questions of your own data:

      • What is the denominator? A count mostly shows where many people live. A rate needs a base, and a tiny base makes wild rates.
      • What is the unit? A coloured area is not the people in it. Large, empty areas can dominate the picture.
      • What is missing, and is missing zero? Decide for each gap: zero, not available, or suppressed. Say it in the legend.

      Whatever you map, write down your choices (classification, speed, buffer width, date of the data). The number depends on them.
